### Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi\u2019s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough

Filed as: Edition No. 29 — The Midday Watch · 2026-11-10T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-10-midday-watch.html

The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi’s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough

 The news at midday: the morning’s one scheduled number came in a tenth hotter than the morning expected it, on both measures; the morning’s one scheduled witness answered his accusers for twenty-five minutes and the vote on him moved up a day; the market that rose on Monday gave back part of the rise at the open and then steadied on a filing; and the two tables the week opened—Abu Dhabi and Paris—produced a duration, a seating plan and no agreement by noon.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 28, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 27, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday corrected the morning on the number, on the vote, and on the speaker, and it left every negotiation and every count exactly where the night left them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put October’s consumer prices up 0.4 percent on the month and core prices up 0.3 percent, in the Reuters account filed below; the overnight edition carried a consensus of 0.3 and 0.2, and the correction is a tenth on each measure, stated in the section below. At the Pentagon, Secretary Hegseth held his first press conference since May and called Representative Massie’s eight articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage, in the Washington account filed below; Mr. Massie answered that the House votes today, on a procedural motion first, with votes expected at 1730—not Wednesday, as the midnight file had it. In New York the three main indexes opened lower, the ten-year yield stood near 4.99 percent, and Brent crude traded below ninety dollars for the first time since August, before the Anthropic filing, printed below, steadied the technology shares by mid-morning. In Abu Dhabi the first day of the three-way talks ended after nearly four hours and resumes Wednesday, with no breakthrough announced. In Jerusalem the opposition named its candidate for speaker, Matan Kahana of Yashar, and the 26th Knesset opened in the afternoon with Speaker Ohana taking the oath and the chair. Neither Senate race was called by noon, and no new figure for either was published in the morning.

The Correction at Noon: The Number Came In a Tenth Hot on Both Measures

The day’s first official statement was a number, and the number corrects the consensus this paper printed at 0400. The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said in its release; core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as they did in September and in August—a third straight month at that rate, in the bureau’s figures as carried and the release account filed below. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent on the headline and 0.2 percent on the core. The overnight edition carried that consensus; the print is a tenth above it on both measures, and the desk files the correction at the head of the edition, where corrections belong. Inside the index: energy rose 0.7 percent, against 5.2 percent in September, with gasoline up 1.0 percent against 9.1 percent; food rose 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent; shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; real average hourly earnings were unchanged on the month. No annual rate was published, for the reason the overnight edition gave: the bureau collected no October 2025 data during last year’s lapse in appropriations, so there is no October-to-October comparison to print. September’s annual rate, 3.7 percent, remains a September figure. The next report, covering November, is scheduled for December 10—one day after the Federal Reserve meeting this report now feeds.

The print met, exactly, the test a governor of the Federal Reserve had set for it four and a half hours before it landed. Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London in remarks published at 0900 GMT, said he was leaning toward supporting a 25-basis-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting even if October improved on September, and that if core prices rose around 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point increase should be considered, because hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk, in the London account and the remarks account filed below. Core printed 0.3 percent. The governor’s condition is therefore met on his own stated terms; the committee’s decision is not his alone and has not been taken. The market’s pricing moved in the same direction before and after the release: traders priced an almost 99 percent chance of a December increase in one account filed below, fully priced two quarter-point increases by March in another, and had priced better than 80 percent for December before the print. The accounts differ on the instrument and the hour; they agree on the direction, and the desk prints the agreement and the differing figures in the Cocked Hat.

Washington at Noon: Twenty-Five Minutes at the Pentagon, a Vote at 1730

Secretary Hegseth answered the articles the way the articles were filed—in public, by name, and without conceding any of them. In his first Pentagon press conference since May—six months in the Associated Press count, 180 days in the count this paper has carried—the secretary said no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached in 250 years for carrying out lawful military operations, that the effort is about policy disagreements and not high crimes, and that his accuser is a rogue lawmaker, in the Associated Press account filed below. The other accounts carry the same sentences in his sharper words: a farce and a stunt, in the Reuters account; “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” in the briefing account; and, on the troops, that anyone coming for the warriors would have to come through him, in the Pentagon account filed below. On the record he defends, he cited Operation Epic Fury’s more than 13,000 targets struck and the destruction of Iran’s navy and of more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base; those are the secretary’s figures, printed as his. The conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and took a handful of questions. The articles themselves are unchanged since Monday: three charging the Iran campaign under the War Powers Resolution, and the rest covering the school strike at Minab, the vessel strikes, Venezuela, Yemen, and the alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly. They are allegations in a charging document, found by no court.

The second correction of the day is the House’s clock. The midnight edition carried House leaders as having until Wednesday to table, refer or vote. On Tuesday morning Representative Massie posted that the House votes today: the first vote is on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, such as a motion to refer it to committee, and if that effort is overcome the House proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles, in the schedule account and the Reuters account filed below. The daily schedule Mr. Massie shared puts the House in at 1000 for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 1730. At noon the procedural motion stands listed and unvoted. A simple majority impeaches in the House; conviction and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 seats in the accounts filed below. Whatever Tuesday evening decides, the accounts agree the effort returns in January if it fails now, when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: A Hotter Print, a Lower Open, and Oil Below Ninety

Wall Street’s reading of the morning was given at the open, and it was a partial retraction of Monday, not a reversal of it. The Dow fell 226.5 points, or 0.43 percent, at the open to 52,163.21; the S&P 500 fell 36.8 points, or 0.49 percent, to 7,513.09; and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 205.7 points, or 0.81 percent, to 25,047.448, in the Reuters snapshot filed below. A second snapshot at 0948 ran a touch lower on all three—the Dow down 0.47 percent, the S&P 500 down 0.58 percent, the Nasdaq down 0.70 percent—with the ten-year Treasury yield at 4.988 percent, up from Monday’s close of 4.862 percent, in the early-session account filed below. Nvidia fell 2.6 percent in one opening account and 1.6 percent in a pre-open account; the chip shares that led Monday’s rise gave back part of it. Europe, which had risen into the number—the FTSE 100 up 0.5 percent at London’s midday, the CAC 40 up 1.2 percent and the DAX up 1.3 percent, in the London midday account filed below—pared its gains after it. Oil completed the morning’s sentence: Brent fell more than 3 percent and traded below ninety dollars a barrel for the first time since late August, at $89.88 in one account, with West Texas Intermediate down more than 2 percent to below $85, in the global markets account filed below. The same barrel that settled at $92.57 on Monday has now fallen through two round numbers in two days, on the same cause the accounts have named throughout: a president holding off further strikes on Iran.

By mid-morning the fall had steadied, and the steadying had a name. Both Nasdaq indexes erased their opening losses and traded into positive territory as attention shifted to Anthropic’s planned listing, before backing off to stand near unchanged, in the rebound account filed below. The filing behind the move is the morning’s second large document. Anthropic, in an updated prospectus filed Tuesday, will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 a share, raising $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion, at a valuation of up to $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, in the filing account filed below; the Reuters accounts put the non-diluted value at about $1 trillion to $1.02 trillion, the difference being the treatment of options and restricted stock, in the Reuters account and the exclusive account filed below. A separate $26 billion private placement with cornerstone investors including Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices stands beside the offering. The terms filed Tuesday are lower than the terms briefly circulated to bankers on Monday night and retracted—about 867 million shares at up to $80—and lower than the $2 trillion discussed earlier in the year, against a May private valuation of $965 billion. Run-rate revenue stood at $81 billion at the end of October. Trading is expected on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT near November 19. On the morning the print argued for dearer money, the largest test of the AI boom priced itself anyway, at a lower price than it first asked.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Four Hours, a Framework Proposed, and the Land Left for Wednesday

The talks the overnight edition filed as open are, at noon, adjourned for the day, and the day produced a duration and a method and no result. The first day concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti account said, and the talks are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in the Associated Press account filed below. The day’s order is on the record: it began with a meeting of the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, and then moved to the trilateral format with Russia. Mr. Kushner, opening, said the United States wanted to draw lessons from previous efforts and develop a new structure, and Washington is pressing a new European security framework, in the framework account filed below. One account citing an American official puts day one on policing a future ceasefire, with territory waiting until day two, and reports the same official saying both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, in the running-order account filed below. That flexibility rests on one unnamed official’s briefing and is printed as such. The stated positions have not moved in public, and no breakthrough has been announced by any delegation. The desk files four hours, a framework proposed, and the land question carried to Wednesday.

Paris at Noon: The Second Day, Ukraine’s Minister in the Room, No Statement in the File

The G7’s two days in Paris ran out at midday with the argument it opened with, now spoken by the guest as well as the hosts. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, joined Tuesday’s session on Ukraine—air defence, economic pressure, Black Sea navigation—having said before departing, “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” in the Paris account filed below. Germany’s sentence stands: Europe belongs at this table, and no fundamental change to Europe’s security architecture is necessary, right or appropriate—an answer, in substance, to the framework Mr. Kushner proposed in Abu Dhabi the same morning. France’s stands: Europeans will participate in the Abu Dhabi discussions. The Kremlin’s stands against both: the negotiations remain trilateral. The Abu Dhabi lists at noon agree with the Kremlin on the main table and with France on the rooms around it. The second session took up instability in the Middle East, with the European ministers warning against renewed American strikes on Iran and arguing for restoring normal shipping through Hormuz, in the ministers account filed below. Canada announced fresh sanctions on Russia on Monday. France had indicated the meeting might produce no joint statement; at noon none is in the file, and the desk files its absence as an absence, not as a rupture.

Jerusalem at Noon: A Candidate Named, an Oath Taken, and the Chair Held for Now

Jerusalem supplied the day’s third correction: the unnamed speaker of the overnight file has a name. The opposition bloc on Tuesday chose former minister Matan Kahana of Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party as its candidate for speaker, to replace Amir Ohana of Likud, in the candidate account filed below. The naming settles the question the mandate carried from Sunday—who, if the chair changes hands—and leaves the other two open: at least 61 members must sign or vote for a replacement, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc stands at 48, and Mr. Ohana has said he will not hold the vote on inauguration day but will schedule it within the following week on a valid request. The ceremony itself ran on its printed schedule: a plaza ceremony at 1520 Jerusalem time and the plenary at 1600, which is 0900 in Washington. In the opening broadcast account, President Herzog addressed the session, called on lawmakers to debate with respect, and invited Speaker Ohana to take the oath before handing him the chair; Mr. Ohana pledged, Psalm 122 was recited, and the roll-call pledges of the 120 members proceeded under his chairmanship, with one warning issued to a member over an interruption, in the opening account filed below. The account itself cautions that the broadcast segments reviewed do not establish that all 120 oaths were completed, and the desk prints the caution with the fact. Mr. Ohana’s assumption of the chair for the opening is a step in the ceremony, not the outcome of the speaker question; Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister, and the mandate runs to December 6. One figure in the file disagrees with itself: the overnight edition carried 47 first-time members, and Tuesday’s candidate account carries 46. The desk prints both in the Cocked Hat and settles neither.

Iran at Noon: No New Sentence, and a Barrel Below Ninety as the Market’s Translation

Neither capital added a sentence to the Iran file in the morning, and the file at noon is the standing one, with one price changed underneath it. The president’s position stands as Monday’s: fresh strikes held off for now after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait; the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate kept in place; forces locked and loaded if the position changes, in the Reuters account and the pause account filed below. Tehran’s two registers stand: negotiate with dignity, from its president; imaginary talks and the seven conditions, from its security council secretary. Secretary Rubio’s sentence stands against both: no progress, and the demands not realistic. One unconfirmed report in the morning file says, on unnamed sources, that the United States is prepared to let Iran keep enriching uranium at 3.67 percent and that Tehran is willing to accept that limit; neither government has confirmed it, and the desk files it as one unconfirmed report, not as a term. The movement in the file is financial, not verbal: Brent’s fall below ninety dollars is the market’s translation of the pause. What the two capitals agree on remains what they agreed on at midnight: the blockade exists. It is imposed in one account and demanded lifted in the other, and it stood all morning.

Krak&oacute;w at Noon: The Autopsies’ Second Day, and No Findings Published

Krak&oacute;w’s file at noon is an instrument running, not a result. The autopsies of the nine victims, begun Monday, were expected to take about two days, which puts their completion at about today; no findings from them had been published by noon, and the desk does not fill the space where findings will go. The standing facts are Monday’s: the suspect died at about 0430 on Monday after at least three operations; the case against the dead man will in time be closed while the investigation around him—whether he acted alone or was inspired, the phones, computers and 11 firearms under analysis—continues; and the prosecutors’ limit stands, that they have no findings that would let them state responsibly that he was inspired by any particular ideology. The interior ministry’s review of gun licensing, announced after police data showed more than 50,000 new licences issued in 2025, is the file’s one new policy instrument; both the gunman and his father held permits. The city’s own mourning runs through tomorrow, November 11. The wounded stand at 15 in hospital in the governor’s count, against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count; the disagreement is carried in the Cocked Hat, as it has been since Monday.

The Count at Noon: Both Deadlines Fall Today, and No New Figure by Noon

For a sixth day neither Senate race was called, and the morning published no new figure for either race; Tuesday’s part in both files is deadlines, not numbers, until the counts run. Alaska’s next scheduled count falls today, carrying early votes cast October 30 to November 2, absentee and questioned ballots, on a race standing in the last state posting at Mary Peltola 102,962 to Dan Sullivan 102,325—a margin of 637 first-choice votes, with no candidate near 50 percent and the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18. A running results account updated Tuesday carries the same race in rounder figures as of November 9—Ms. Peltola at 48.6 percent to Mr. Sullivan’s 47.5 percent, more than 220,000 ballots counted and about 78.5 percent of ballots in, in the running account filed below; the percentages and the raw posting are two printings of one standing count, not two counts. Mississippi’s deadlines fall today: mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and affidavit voters must cure their identification, on a race standing at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on about 97 percent counted in the Associated Press estimate; the same running account carries Mississippi in percentages as 49.1 to 48.8 with 99 percent counted, a figure the desk cannot reconcile with the 97 percent estimate and prints as a disagreement in the Cocked Hat, in the delay account filed below. Counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. Alaska’s count, when it posts, will move in the state’s afternoon, which is Washington’s evening; the midday file therefore closes the count where the night left it, with both of its named days arrived and neither of its numbers yet moved. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the December increase, almost 99 percent in one pricing account, fully priced by March in another, and better than 80 percent before the print in a third—three instruments, one direction. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $1.02 trillion not diluted: a difference of definition, printed as one. On the open, the Reuters snapshot and the 0948 snapshot differing by tenths on all three indexes, as snapshots an hour apart will. On Abu Dhabi’s flexibility, one unnamed official’s briefing against every delegation’s public silence. On the enrichment report, one unconfirmed account against no confirmation from either capital. On Jerusalem’s new members, 47 in the overnight file and 46 in Tuesday’s candidate account. On Mississippi’s completeness, about 97 percent in the wire estimate and 99 percent in the running account, irreconcilable at noon. On Krak&oacute;w’s wounded, 15 in the governor’s hospital count against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count. Against the triangle, the midday’s single-valued facts are these: prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent in October, a tenth hot on both measures against the consensus, with no annual rate in existence; Governor Waller’s stated condition for considering a half-point increase was met by the core print; Secretary Hegseth spoke for about 25 minutes and conceded nothing; the House’s first vote on his articles is set for Tuesday evening; Brent traded below ninety dollars; Anthropic filed at $70 to $78; Abu Dhabi’s first day ran nearly four hours and produced no announced breakthrough; Matan Kahana is the opposition’s candidate for speaker and Amir Ohana holds the chair; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to the evening.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters, via SRN News — a hot October inflation report rattles marketsUnited States consumer prices increased more than expected in October, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September; economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent. Core prices rose 0.3 percent, against a forecast of 0.2 percent. The bureau did not publish year-over-year readings because last year’s shutdown prevented collection of October 2025 data; annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September. Governor Waller, the account notes, had said the central bank ought to raise borrowing costs in December even if inflation cooled.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine — consumer inflation slows to 0.4 percent in October as energy pressures easeThe Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core inflation was unchanged at 0.3 percent, the same rate as September and August. Energy prices increased 0.7 percent, sharply slower than September’s 5.2 percent rise; food prices rose 0.5 percent after remaining unchanged in September. No annual rate was published, because comparable October 2025 data were unavailable following the lapse in appropriations.

 SubjectiveUSA Today — inflation slowed in October, but annual data is missing after the shutdownConsumer prices climbed 0.4 percent in October, down from 0.6 percent in September and higher than forecasters expected; the Cleveland Fed’s nowcast had projected 0.24 percent. Core inflation rose 0.3 percent. The report is the last look at consumer prices the Federal Reserve will get before its December meeting, and one economist quoted says it most likely seals a rate increase to close the year. The account carries the gasoline figures: regular gasoline up 34 percent and diesel up 64 percent since February 28, on AAA data, with the national average at $3.98 on November 10.

 SubjectiveSHRM — inflation continued to rise in OctoberThe consumer price index increased 0.4 percent in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on November 10, higher than the 0.3 percent economists expected. Shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; food increased 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent and food away from home up 0.5 percent; energy increased 0.7 percent after jumping 5.2 percent in September. Real average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October.

 SubjectiveZacks — pre-markets drop on warmer CPI numbersPre-market futures swung lower ahead of the opening bell on October consumer prices of plus 0.4 percent on the month, 20 basis points below September’s 0.6 percent and 10 above consensus; core came in at plus 0.3 percent, also 10 hotter than expected. Bond yields climbed with the numbers: 4.936 percent on the ten-year, 4.627 percent on the two-year and 5.292 percent on the thirty-year, in the account’s prints. The small-business optimism index for October ticked down to 97.8.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine, carrying Reuters — Governor Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in DecemberFederal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support raising short-term borrowing costs next month even if the data showed inflation cooled, and would consider an upsized half-point increase if the picture worsened. If core consumer prices rise 0.3 percent or more from September, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered at the December meeting, he said, adding that hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk. Markets, the account says, had priced in about an 85 percent chance of a December increase to a 4.00 to 4.25 percent range.

 SubjectiveAmerican Banker — Governor Waller calls for raising interest rates 25 basis points, at leastGovernor Waller, in prepared remarks delivered in London on Tuesday morning, said he anticipates supporting a rate increase at the December meeting even if the consumer price print improves, and that if October’s monthly reading comes in at or above September’s level a 50-basis-point increase should be considered. The account’s key insight is that one of the Board’s leading monetary experts is committed to a December increase and could support a half-point move. He cited concern at the breadth of price increases, including core goods and core market-based services excluding housing.

 SubjectiveAssociated Press, via Military.com — Secretary Hegseth says the impeachment push is about policy disagreements, not high crimesWASHINGTON (AP): Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dug in for a fight on Tuesday against his potential impeachment, telling reporters a rogue lawmaker is targeting him over policy disagreements and not the high crimes the founders intended. In the 250 years of the republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, he said. The briefing was his first from the Pentagon in six months. Representative Massie, who lost his primary to a president-backed opponent, filed the resolution on Monday; it focuses largely on the Iran war and includes Yemen and Venezuela.

It’s a political spectacle,” he said. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.” The news conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and ended after he took a handful of questions, mostly from reporters representing conservative media outlets, in the account’s description. The House was planning to vote on whether to move forward later on November 10.

He made the comment at a news conference a day after Representative Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him, in his first Pentagon news conference since May. In a post on X, Mr. Massie said the House would hold a first vote on Tuesday on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, and that if that effort is overcome, the House will proceed to a real debate and a vote on the articles.

 SubjectiveNew York Post — Secretary Hegseth rips the impeachment effort in his first press conference since MayThe secretary went on a fiery tirade on Tuesday against Representative Massie over his bid to impeach him, accusing the rogue legislator of sabotage: “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage.” He insisted he has done nothing worthy of being just the third cabinet official in history to be impeached. The articles announced Monday include three charges over the war in Iran, one on the operation to capture Venezuela’s leader, one on attacks against the Houthis in Yemen, one on ignoring laws aimed at minimizing civilian casualties, one for extrajudicial killings on alleged drug boats, and one for free-speech violations against Senator Kelly.

 SubjectiveDefense News — Secretary Hegseth denounces the farce impeachment in his first briefing since MayThe secretary vehemently defended himself on Tuesday against impending impeachment proceedings, listing military successes in his first Pentagon press briefing in over six months. The conference lasted fewer than 25 minutes and he answered few questions. The articles, he said, are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize the military. He painted himself as a champion for the troops, saying that if they want to come for the warriors, they will have to come through him. He praised Operation Epic Fury, claiming Iran’s navy and more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base were destroyed. Speaker Johnson will decide if lawmakers vote on each article individually or all eight as a whole, the account says.

 SubjectiveMilitary.com — Secretary Hegseth claims an Iran victory in the press conference as the war and impeachment fight continueThe secretary defended the administration’s military campaigns on Tuesday morning, declaring the president had kicked their teeth in in Iran and promising that anyone pursuing American service members would have to come through him. He celebrated Operation Epic Fury as a historic victory, citing more than 13,000 targets struck, extensive damage to Iran’s military infrastructure and destruction of much of its nuclear industrial capacity. The account notes the resolution seeks to impeach him as a civilian cabinet secretary and does not charge service members, and that the allegations concern his responsibility, including three articles alleging violations of the War Powers Resolution.

 SubjectiveANI, via APNA MA TV — “Today the House will vote,” Representative Massie saysRepresentative Thomas Massie said on Tuesday the House of Representatives would vote on his impeachment resolution against Secretary Hegseth, with an initial procedural vote expected to determine whether it proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles. The first vote would concern a procedural motion aimed at blocking the resolution, including a possible motion to refer it to committee. The daily legislative schedule for Tuesday, November 10 listed the procedural motion among the day’s business; the House was due at 10 a.m. for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 5:30 p.m.

 SubjectiveReuters, via DevDiscourse — a defiant Secretary Hegseth blasts the impeachment effort ahead of the House voteThe secretary on Tuesday blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce that would embolden adversaries, as the House scheduled a procedural vote for late Tuesday that will test support for the impeachment. Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with the president’s Republicans still controlling the House until the new Congress takes over on January 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, the account says, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.

 SubjectiveAssociated Press, via WNCW — Russia and Ukraine hold nearly four hours of United States-mediated talks in Abu DhabiABU DHABI: three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the Emirates, the first such meeting since February, in a two-day session focused on security guarantees. The first day of talks concluded after nearly four hours, RIA Novosti said; they are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service. Mr. Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, before the trilateral format.

 SubjectiveNational Daily — the United States pushes a new European security framework as the talks begin in Abu DhabiUnited States-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with Washington pushing for a new European security framework aimed at ending the war and preventing future conflicts. Opening the negotiations, Mr. Kushner said the United States wanted to develop a new framework by examining previous diplomatic arrangements and identifying what had worked and failed. Ukraine’s delegation, led by Mr. Umerov, began the day with discussions involving American representatives and European officials before moving into the trilateral format with Russia. The talks take place amid continued military operations, with both countries reporting overnight drone and missile attacks.

 SubjectiveIl Politico — Abu Dhabi peace talks: security guarantees before territoryThe round runs Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, the first since February, when talks in Geneva broke up without a deal on land. Day one is about policing a future ceasefire and the shape of security once the guns fall silent; territory waits until day two, according to Bloomberg citing an American official. The same official told Reuters both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, and that any deal on land would come at the very end, once everything else is settled. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the talks are trilateral, full stop.

 SubjectiveGrenada Chronicle — “Europe belongs at this table,” Germany tells the United States before the Ukraine talksEuropean foreign ministers told Secretary Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end the war, on Monday in Paris at the G7 meeting. “It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said after talks with Mr. Rubio; “Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.” The two-day Paris meeting ends Tuesday and overlaps the Abu Dhabi talks. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, is set to join a session on Ukraine on Tuesday; “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” he said before departing. Iran is expected to feature prominently in Tuesday’s discussions.

 SubjectiveEurope Says — G7 ministers press Secretary Rubio on Iran and Ukraine at the Paris talksPARIS: G7 top diplomats began a two-day meeting in Paris on Monday, with European foreign ministers set to press Secretary Rubio to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine and to steer clear of any new escalation with Iran. French Foreign Minister Jean-No&euml;l Barrot said Europeans would be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating. European ministers warned against renewed American military strikes and advocated instead for the restoration of normal commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. ### Donald J. Trump: The Documented Record, 1946 to 2026

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-10T11:50:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-10-trump-biography.html

Special Report

 An Objective Biography—Origins, the Building Business, the Brand, Two Presidencies, the Courts, and the Money

 Objective

 Donald J. Trump: The Documented Record, 1946 to 2026 — Special Report

 Donald John Trump, born June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York, is the 45th and 47th President of the United States, the only president impeached twice, and the first former president convicted of a felony. This report files his documented record whole, from the record and not from either camp’s telling of it: the Queens real-estate family and the disputed size of the father’s money; the education and the Vietnam-era draft file; the building career, the $3.4 billion debt workout of 1990, and the six corporate Chapter 11 filings that stand beside the documented fact that he never filed for bankruptcy personally; the brand era of The Apprentice, licensing, Trump University, and the Trump Foundation; three marriages and the personal record; the 2016 election, the Mueller report in its own words, two impeachments and two acquittals, the 2020 election and January 6; the four criminal cases of 2023 and their four different ends—one conviction, argued on appeal on November 5, 2026, with no decision issued as this report files, and three dismissals; the two Carroll verdicts and the New York fraud judgment, whose $464 million penalty stands vacated on appeal while its liability finding stands affirmed, the whole case now before the state’s highest court undecided; the 2024 election and the second term’s orders, tariffs, wars, and shutdown, and the 2026 midterm elections, called for the Democratic Party in both chambers of Congress with two Senate races uncalled and no state certification yet issued; and the money, kept throughout in the three separate ledgers the record itself keeps it in—his own claims, the estimators’ published figures, and the courts’ findings. Allegations are attributed, denials are carried, adjudicated outcomes are stated as outcomes, and where the record disagrees with itself the disagreement is printed, not averaged.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1150 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026.

The File in Brief

The man first, because everything else in this file is downstream of him. Donald John Trump was born on June 14, 1946, in Jamaica Hospital, Queens, the fourth of five children of Fred Trump, a builder of middle-income housing in Brooklyn and Queens, and Mary Anne MacLeod Trump, a Scottish immigrant who arrived in New York in 1930 with a domestic worker’s visa. He was sent at thirteen to the New York Military Academy, attended Fordham University for two years, and took a bachelor’s degree in economics from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania in 1968. He never served in the armed forces: the Selective Service record documents four student deferments, a medical classification of 1-Y in October 1968 attributed by Trump to bone spurs, a draft-lottery number, 356, too high to be called, and a permanent 4-F classification in 1972. The diagnosis behind the medical classification is not documented; the reporting on it is contested; both facts are printed in section 3. He took the presidency of his father’s company in 1971, moved its ambitions from the outer boroughs to Manhattan, and built the public identity—developer, casino operator, television host, licensor of his own name—on which, in 2015, he opened a campaign for the presidency. He has been married three times and has five children. He is, as this report files, the sitting President of the United States, twenty-two months into a second term that the midterm elections of November 3, 2026, have just answered with a Congress of the opposite party.

The father’s money is the first contested number in the file, and the contest is between a framing and a document review. Trump’s own account, given in 2015 and repeated since, is that his father gave him “a small loan of a million dollars,” repaid with interest. The New York Times’ investigation of October 2, 2018, built on more than 100,000 pages of Fred Trump’s tax returns and financial records, found transfers of at least $413 million in 2018 dollars across Donald Trump’s lifetime, loans of at least $60.7 million mostly never repaid, and a child who was a millionaire in inflation-adjusted terms by age eight. The family and the White House denied the investigation’s tax-scheme characterizations as “100 percent false”; the transfer figures themselves were never rebutted with documents, and no official disposition of the state tax review announced the same day has ever been published. The report prints the range, $1 million as the framing of one loan and $413 million as the documented-review total of all transfers, and does not split it.

The business record is a rise, a collapse that stopped one step short of personal ruin, and a reinvention as a licensor. The documented spine: the Grand Hyatt conversion of 1980 and Trump Tower in 1983 made him a Manhattan figure; the Atlantic City casinos and the Plaza Hotel made him, by 1990, a debtor of about $3.4 billion on the New Jersey regulators’ count, $832.5 million of it personally guaranteed, kept from personal bankruptcy by a bank workout that capped his personal spending and took mortgages on nearly everything he owned. Six Chapter 11 petitions by Trump-controlled entities followed between 1991 and 2009; in each, the property kept operating, creditors took less than face value, and his ownership fell. He has never filed a personal bankruptcy petition; that sentence and the six filings are both the record, and the report prints them together, as it prints his own statement—“I have never gone bankrupt”—beside them. The public casino company, DJT, lost money in every year of its existence, about $640 million cumulatively, while paying him more than $44 million on one review of its filings. The Apprentice, from 2004, rebuilt the fortune on fame: about $197 million in salary and fees on the tax records the Times examined, and about $230 million more in the licensing income the fame generated. Trump University ended in a $25 million settlement in November 2016, its fraud allegations never adjudicated; the Trump Foundation ended dissolved under court supervision, with a $2 million court-ordered payment and nineteen paragraphs of admissions in the settlement stipulations.

The legal record of the 2020s is the densest part of the file, and its state at filing is this. Of the four criminal cases brought in 2023, one produced a conviction: a Manhattan jury’s unanimous verdict on May 30, 2024, on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records, followed on January 10, 2025, by a sentence of unconditional discharge—the conviction final, the punishment none. His appeal was argued before a five-judge panel of the Appellate Division, First Department, on November 5, 2026; the desk’s pre-publication check of November 10 finds no decision issued, and none is claimed here. The two federal cases were dismissed after the 2024 election under the Justice Department’s policy against prosecuting a sitting president, the documents case on a judge’s ruling that the special counsel’s appointment was unconstitutional, its merits never reached; the Georgia case was dismissed in full on November 26, 2025, by the successor prosecutor after the elected district attorney’s disqualification. The civil record stands differently: two juries found against him for E. Jean Carroll—sexual abuse and defamation, $5 million in 2023; defamation, $83.3 million in 2024—and both judgments were affirmed on appeal; the $5 million judgment is final, the Supreme Court having denied review on June 29, 2026, while the $83.3 million judgment is before that Court now, its enforcement stayed. A New York judge’s finding of persistent fraud in his financial statements stands affirmed; the $464 million penalty that accompanied it was vacated in August 2025 as an excessive fine; both sides have carried the case to the New York Court of Appeals, where, the desk’s check finds, it stands briefed and undecided, seventeen state attorneys general having filed in support of the state on November 5, 2026. Beyond Carroll, accusations of sexual misconduct by other women are counted by their counters at between 16 and 28; all are alleged, all are denied, none has produced a criminal charge, and Carroll’s is the only one adjudicated. Section 10 files the whole docket, matter by matter.

The political record is two presidencies separated by a defeat he has never conceded. He won the presidency in 2016 while losing the popular vote by 2.87 million; lost it in 2020 by 7.06 million votes and 306 to 232 in the Electoral College; and won it back in 2024 with 312 electoral votes and a popular-vote plurality of 2.28 million, the first non-consecutive return since Grover Cleveland. Between the defeat and the return stand the documented events of January 6, 2021—a riot at the Capitol during the electoral count, five deaths in the medical examiner’s count for the two days, about 140 injured police officers, a second impeachment, and a Senate vote of 57 to 43 for conviction, ten short—and, in January 2025, his own proclamation pardoning nearly all of those convicted for that day. The Mueller investigation’s two operative sentences are printed verbatim in section 8: on coordination, the investigation “did not establish” it; on obstruction, the report “does not exonerate him.” His first-term Gallup average, 41 percent, is the lowest full-term average in that series, and he is the only president in the series never to reach 50 percent. The second term, through this filing, contains 274 executive orders by August 2026 on the Federal Register’s numbering, a reconciliation statute carrying a $5 trillion debt-limit increase, a tariff program the Supreme Court held unlawful under its stated authority on February 20, 2026, the longest government shutdown on record at 43 days, two wars against Iran in the record’s count, and immigration enforcement whose own administration counts more than 3 million departures against independent estimates near 1 million, the range printed with its holders. On November 3, 2026, the voters took both chambers of Congress from his party; the desk’s pre-publication check finds the Associated Press’s calls standing—Democrats at 54 Senate seats with two races uncalled, and past the 218-seat House majority with about twenty races uncalled—and no state’s certification yet issued, the first county certifications falling due November 13. The numbers in this paragraph that are projections are labeled as projections in section 11, and nothing in this report treats an uncalled race as decided.

The money, in sum, is three numbers that are not one number. His own claims run from $8,737,540,000 in his 2015 campaign release to “in excess of TEN BILLION DOLLARS” in his own announcement of it, and include his sworn deposition testimony of 2007 that his net worth goes up and down “with attitudes and with feelings, even my own feelings.” The estimators’ figures run from Forbes’s $200 million family-share entry in 1982, through removal from the Forbes 400 for 1990 to 1995, $4.5 billion from Forbes and about $3 billion from Bloomberg at the first campaign, a decline to about $2.1 to $2.5 billion across the first term, and a rise on the Trump Media listing and the crypto ventures to Forbes’s highest figure for him, $7.3 billion in September 2025, and $7.0 billion in September 2026, with Bloomberg’s latest cited reading at about $7.1 billion. The courts’ figure is of a different kind: an adjudicated finding that the statements of financial condition issued in his name overstated his assets and net worth, by $812 million to $2.2 billion in given years on the Attorney General’s figures, which the trial court substantially credited. No audited personal balance sheet exists in the public record to reconcile the three ledgers, and this report does not pretend one does. His 2025 financial disclosure, released in June 2026, reported more than $2.2 billion of income in a year, more than $1.4 billion of it crypto-related—an income figure, printed as one, and not a net worth.

1. Origins: Fred Trump, Mary Anne MacLeod, and the Queens Upbringing

The paternal line begins in Kallstadt, in the Palatinate. Friedrich Trump emigrated to the United States in 1885, made money in the restaurant and hotel trade of the Pacific Northwest and the Klondike, returned to Germany to marry, and was ordered expelled by Bavaria in 1905 for having emigrated without completing military service; the family settled in Queens. His son Fred, born in 1905 in the Bronx, began building houses in Queens as a teenager in his mother’s company, Elizabeth Trump & Son, and became one of New York’s largest builders of middle-income housing—garden apartments in Brooklyn and Queens by the tens of thousands of units, financed substantially with federal housing money, and held, as a rule, rather than sold. Fred Trump’s method is documented in the assessments of his own era: low cost, tight management, political fluency, and rents kept at the level his tenants could pay. His own controversies are part of the record the son inherited: a 1954 Senate Banking Committee inquiry into windfall profits on FHA-insured projects, in which Fred Trump testified and was not charged; and, in 1927, his arrest at a Ku Klux Klan parade riot in Queens, a documented arrest in the police record of the event, the charge dismissed—filed here as an arrest record, which is all it is, with no finding attached to it in either direction.

Mary Anne MacLeod was born in 1912 in Tong, on the Isle of Lewis in Scotland, the youngest of ten children of a fisherman and crofter. She immigrated in May 1930, her visa numbered 26698, entered for domestic service, became a naturalized citizen in 1942, and married Fred Trump in 1936. The couple had five children: Maryanne, a federal judge; Fred Jr., an airline pilot who died in 1981 at 42 of alcoholism-related illness; Elizabeth; Donald, born June 14, 1946; and Robert, who died in 2020. The family lived in Jamaica Estates, Queens, in a brick house Fred Trump built. The household record, as the biographies assembled from family and school sources describe it, was prosperous, disciplined, and competitive; Donald Trump’s own accounts describe a father he admired and a childhood of energy that the family answered, in 1959, by sending the thirteen-year-old to military school. The reason for the enrollment is reported rather than documented—the biographical record, including family accounts, describes a boy whose behavior his parents, and principally his father, judged to need the structure—and it is printed as reported.

Kew-Forest School, in Forest Hills, was his school until 1959. The childhood behavior record rests on the recollections of classmates and teachers collected by biographers decades later; it is consistent in describing a forceful, disruptive, athletic child, and it is recollection, graded as such in the desk’s research file and carried here in one sentence because a biography prints what the record holds and labels what the record is.

2. The Father’s Money

No fact in this file is more argued over relative to its documentary mass than the size of Fred Trump’s support. The two public accounts are these. Donald Trump’s, first given in 2015: “I got a very small loan from my father of one million dollars,” repaid with interest—a framing he has repeated, with the borrowing described against his father’s opposition to the Manhattan move. The New York Times’ account, published October 2, 2018, after a year-long examination of more than 100,000 pages of Fred Trump’s tax returns, partnership documents, bank statements, and audits, confidential records provided to the paper: Fred Trump transferred to his children, and principally to Donald, at least $413 million in 2018 dollars across his lifetime. The components the Times printed include salary from the family company rising to millions a year in the 1980s; loans of at least $60.7 million, most never repaid; trust funds and gifts beginning in childhood—Donald Trump a millionaire, in inflation-adjusted terms, by age eight, drawing the equivalent of about $200,000 a year by then and more than $1 million a year at 22; and crisis support in 1990 and 1991, including a $3.35 million purchase of casino chips by Fred Trump’s lawyer at Trump Castle in December 1990, made without gambling, ahead of a bond payment the casino could not otherwise meet—a transaction New Jersey regulators determined functioned as an unapproved loan, for which the casino admitted a violation and paid a penalty whose components the sources print as $30,000 and $65,000. The Times described the transfer machinery as including discounted partnership interests, inflated invoices through a family purchasing company, and properties passed at understated values. Fred Trump’s estate at his death on June 25, 1999, was estimated by the family at $250 million to $300 million; its value for tax purposes, on the Times’ record analysis, was about $51.8 million. The outer-borough portfolio built by Fred Trump was sold in 2004 for $737.9 million, of which Donald Trump’s share was $177.3 million.

The responses are on the record. The family’s statement in 2018, through a Trump Organization lawyer, called the Times’ tax characterization “highly defamatory and utterly false”; the White House called the report “100 percent false” and a hit piece. Neither response produced documents rebutting the transfer totals. The official aftermath is a null result, printed as one: New York State’s tax department announced a review on the day of publication; no disposition of that review has ever been announced, and the criminal limitations periods applicable to the years in question have expired. The estate itself closed in litigation: Fred Trump’s 1991 will, which cut out the children of Fred Jr., who had died a decade earlier, was contested by Fred Jr.’s son and daughter; the confidential settlement of April 2001 ended the contest, its full terms sealed, the one figure public being more than $2.7 million disclosed by Mary Trump, Fred Jr.’s daughter, in her own later account. The desk’s finding, stated once: the $413 million figure is a reported figure resting on documents the Times examined and quoted; the $1 million figure is the subject’s framing of a single loan; both are printed wherever this report touches the inheritance, and no third figure exists in the record to arbitrate between them.

3. Military School, Fordham, Wharton, and the Draft File

The New York Military Academy, at Cornwall-on-Hudson, held him from 1959 to 1964. The school record documents enrollment, promotion to cadet captain, and participation in sports; the biographical record adds, as reported recollection, a forceful cadet career that included a demotion and a transfer of rooms after an incident with a roommate. He attended Fordham University in the Bronx from 1964 to 1966 and transferred to the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, from which he received a bachelor of science in economics on May 20, 1968. Two education claims require the label treatment. The first is Trump’s repeated statement that he graduated first in his class at Wharton. The 1968 commencement program, a document, lists the honors graduates of his class and his name is not among them; no class ranking placing him first exists in the record. The claim is printed as his statement, contradicted by the program. The second is the mechanism of the transfer itself, which biographers have reported rested in part on an interview arranged through a family friend of an admissions officer; it is reported, not documented, and is carried as such.

The draft file is a Selective Service record, and it is unusually complete. It documents four student deferments, classification 2-S, across 1964 to 1968, the standard deferment of the era for a full-time student. In October 1968, after graduation and two physical examinations, he was classified 1-Y—qualified for service only in time of war or national emergency—on medical grounds. His account, given at various times, is that the ground was bone spurs in his heels; his accounts have varied on the details, including which foot, and he said in 2016 that he could not recall precisely, and later that the spurs were in both feet, and that a doctor provided a letter. On December 1, 1969, the draft lottery assigned his birth date the number 356 of 366, a number never reached; the call that year stopped far below it. On February 1, 1972, his classification became 4-F, permanently unqualified. The diagnosis itself is not documented: Dr. Larry Braunstein, the Queens podiatrist named in the record as the signer of the letter, died in 2007; his daughters told the Times in December 2018 that the examination was, in their father’s telling to the family, a favor to Fred Trump, whose buildings Braunstein rented office space in—family recollection, reported, with no corroborating document, and the Times said so in its own account. Michael Cohen, Trump’s former lawyer, testified to Congress in 2019 that Trump instructed him to handle press inquiries about the draft and that Trump told him “you think I’m stupid” about the prospect of Vietnam—sworn testimony by a witness himself convicted of lying to Congress, printed as testimony, which is what it is. What is documented, and what this report states as the file’s bottom line, is the classifications and the lottery number; what is alleged is the favor; and the two do not occupy the same evidentiary ground, in either direction.

4. The Developer: The Outer Boroughs, the Hyatt, the Tower, Atlantic City

He joined the family company after Wharton and became its president in 1971, at 25; the company took the name the Trump Organization under his presidency, the legal instrument of the renaming not being in the public record. The company’s business was Fred Trump’s: thousands of apartments in Brooklyn and Queens. Its first appearance in the legal record of this biography came in October 1973, when the Department of Justice sued Trump Management for racial discrimination in rentals, alleging that applications from Black renters were marked and steered. The case ended on June 10, 1975, in a consent decree: the company agreed to furnish the Urban League with listings and to rent without regard to race, admitting no liability. Donald Trump’s account, then and since, is that the company settled to avoid an onerous decree and admitted nothing; the government’s complaint and the decree are documents, and the report prints the decree’s terms and the denial together. A 1978 enforcement action followed, the Justice Department alleging the decree was being violated; its formal caption and closure are not settled in the sources the desk could reach, and it is filed here as an open item rather than a finding.

The Manhattan move is the documented break. In 1976 he took an option on the Commodore Hotel, a failing railroad hotel beside Grand Central Terminal, and assembled the financing for its conversion on the strength of a forty-year city tax abatement whose value across its term is estimated by the Times at about $360 million and in other accounts at about $400 million, nominal dollars. The building reopened in 1980 as the Grand Hyatt. Trump Tower followed: the Bonwit Teller site on Fifth Avenue, acquired in 1979, its Art Deco bas-reliefs destroyed in 1980 during demolition after a public dispute over their promised donation to the Metropolitan Museum of Art—Trump’s stated reason at the time was cost and delay, the museum’s position that it would have taken them, both on the record. The tower opened in 1983: 58 stories as counted by its floors’ numbering, which begins at 10, a discrepancy between numbering and structure that is documented and was the first instance of a pattern the record repeats in his building descriptions. His own triplex in it he would later describe, in the financial statements at issue in section 9, as 30,000 square feet; its documented size is 10,996 square feet.

The 1980s expansion ran on borrowed money: the Trump Shuttle airline, bought from Eastern Air Lines in 1989 and surrendered to its lenders in default in 1990; the Plaza Hotel, bought in 1988 for about $390 million, a price Trump himself described at the time as buying a Mona Lisa—“not a real estate investment”—and which the hotel’s cash flow never carried; Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, bought in 1985 and later converted in part to a private club; the Wollman Rink reconstruction of 1986, in which he took over a city project that had run six years and finished it in months under budget, an episode that is documented and that he has cited since as the model of his method; and the United States Football League, whose 1986 antitrust suit against the NFL, in which he was a central owner-advocate, won a verdict of one dollar, trebled to three, and ended the league. Atlantic City was the center of it: the Trump Plaza casino in 1984, the Castle in 1985, and the Taj Mahal, bought unfinished from Resorts International and opened in April 1990 as the largest casino in the world, financed with junk bonds at interest the property could not service from its first year. By the summer of 1990 the structure was insolvent on a cash-flow basis, and the file turns to the workout.

5. The Workout and the Six Filings

The New Jersey Casino Control Commission and the Division of Gaming Enforcement, which had regulatory access to the casino books, put the organization’s total debt in 1990 at about $3.4 billion; other contemporary tallies ran to about $5 billion counting entity and contingent obligations. Of the $3.4 billion, $832.5 million was personally guaranteed by Donald Trump on the Commission’s record, a figure later press summaries put at about $900 million. In June 1990 the organization could not make scheduled payments; nine banks lent a further $65 million in what the Commission called an eleventh-hour save, and in August more than seventy lenders agreed a workout: deferral of principal and reduced interest on about $1 billion of bank debt, second and third mortgages on nearly all his properties, a chief financial officer acceptable to the banks, bank approval over transfers among his companies, and a cap on his personal spending drawn from the businesses—$450,000 a month for the rest of 1990, falling on a schedule to $250,000 a month by 1992. The Trump Shuttle went to its lenders in 1990; the yacht Trump Princess was sold in 1991 to Prince Alwaleed bin Talal for a reported $20 million; the Plaza interest was reduced and sold by 1995. The workout, not any court filing, is what stood between the structure and a personal bankruptcy—a distinction that matters to the next paragraph’s count.

Chapter 11 is a reorganization, not a liquidation: the debtor keeps operating, collection halts, and creditors accept less, later, or in equity. The American Bankruptcy Institute, counting from the dockets, counts six petitions by Trump-controlled entities between 1991 and 2009. They are: Trump Taj Mahal Associates, July 16, 1991, prepackaged, its bondholders taking 50 percent of the casino’s equity for reduced interest and extended maturities; Trump Castle Associates, March 9, 1992, bondholders taking a 50 percent interest on parallel terms; the Trump Plaza casino, March 1992, on the same pattern; the Plaza Hotel’s operating entity, November 1992, carrying more than $550 million of debt, six lenders taking 49 percent, Trump retaining 51 percent on paper with no salary and no operating role; Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts, the public company, November 21, 2004, carrying about $1.8 billion of debt, his ownership falling from 47 percent to 27 percent while other common shareholders were reduced to about 0.05 percent; and Trump Entertainment Resorts, February 17, 2009, filed days after he resigned its chairmanship, from which he emerged in 2010 holding a 10 percent stake paid for the use of his name. A seventh filing, by the same company in 2014 after his control had ended and his stake was extinguished in it, is not counted in the six by the convention the desk follows, and the convention is stated so the count can be checked. Sources that say four group the 1992 filings by event; the docket count is six.

The personal question is answered by the same record. No personal bankruptcy petition by Donald J. Trump—Chapter 7, 11, or 13—appears in the federal court record, and the Institute states the point directly: he has never filed a personal bankruptcy, and his business interests have sought Chapter 11 protection six times. His own statements—“I have never gone bankrupt”; the filings described as the use of “the laws of the country”—are accurate in the narrow legal sense and incomplete as a description of proceedings in which creditors of entities he controlled, chaired, and partly owned accepted losses and equity in place of cash. Both halves are printed because both are in the record. The public company between those filings is its own ledger: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts, taken public in June 1995 at $14 a share under the ticker DJT, bought the Taj Mahal and the Castle from Trump personally in 1996 for a reported $890 million and $485 million, transactions in which he stood on both sides, and then reported a net loss in every year of its existence—about $637 million to $647 million cumulatively on the filings’ reviews, the range a matter of which partial-year lines are counted—while paying him, on a Washington Post review of the same filings, more than $44 million in salary, bonuses, and other payments. A $100 investment in the 1995 offering was worth about $10 by April 2004 on that paper’s calculation. The company’s 2004 filing is the fifth of the six above.

6. The Brand Era: The Apprentice, Licensing, Trump University, the Foundation

The Apprentice premiered on NBC on January 8, 2004, created and co-produced by Mark Burnett, with Trump as host of a business-competition format ending in a boardroom elimination. He hosted fourteen seasons, seven under each title, through February 2015; NBC ended its business relationship with him on June 29, 2015, after the remarks about Mexican immigrants in his campaign announcement. The ratings record is Nielsen’s: the first season averaged 20.7 million viewers and ranked seventh, its finale 28.1 million; the decline ran season by season to his last, which averaged about 7.6 million and ranked 67th. His repeated description of the program, including in its later seasons, as “the No. 1 show on television” is contradicted by those rankings after the first season and is printed as his statement against the instrument. The money, on the two records that hold it: his 2015 Federal Election Commission disclosure reported about $213 million to $214 million of earnings from the show across eleven years; the tax records the Times examined put his direct Apprentice earnings at about $197 million and the licensing and endorsement income the fame generated at about $230 million more. The accounts do not conflict; they cover different periods and categories. The producers’ accounts of the construction are reported, named, and on the record: editors who described “reverse-engineering” episodes so that his boardroom decisions appeared reasoned, a boardroom built as a set on a vacant Trump Tower floor because his offices were judged unsuitable for the image, and, in October 2024, the apology of John D. Miller, the NBC marketing chief who wrote that the network had “created the narrative that Trump was a super-successful businessman who lived like royalty” and called it at best a substantial exaggeration. Burnett himself has given no comparable on-the-record account. The predicate fact for the word rehabilitation, where this report uses it as the producers’ frame and not the desk’s, is documented in the tax records: in the year before the premiere his core businesses had reported $89.9 million in net losses, and ten months after it his casino holding company entered Chapter 11.

The business model of the era was licensing: from the late 1980s, and dominantly after 2004, his entities sold the use of his name—an upfront fee, royalties on condominium sales or hotel revenue, and, in hotel deals, a separate management contract—contributing no land, no construction capital, and no equity, and bearing no construction debt, on the agreements that litigation has made public. The name on a building is therefore not, by itself, evidence of ownership, in either direction: Trump Tower and the golf portfolio were owned; many condominium and hotel projects carrying the name, in the United States and abroad, were licensed. Product licensing ran alongside: Trump Steaks, withdrawn within months in 2007 after, in the Sharper Image chief executive’s words, selling “almost no steaks”; Trump Vodka, Trump Mortgage, a magazine, a travel site, bottled water—the list is documented and most of its members are defunct. The Times’ tax-record analysis attributed about $230 million of licensing and endorsement income to the post-Apprentice years, including $8.8 million from ACN, a multi-level marketing company he endorsed in paid speeches.

Trump University was incorporated in New York in 2004, 93 percent his, and launched on May 23, 2005, selling real-estate seminars—a free session, a three-day seminar at about $1,495, mentoring packages to $34,995. It was not an accredited university and granted no degrees; the state Education Department told it in May 2005 that the word “university” and unlicensed operation violated state law, and it operated under the name until 2010. In 2014 a New York judge held him personally liable for operating without the required license. Three actions followed—two California class actions and the New York Attorney General’s suit, which alleged an elaborate bait-and-switch: instruction promised as handpicked by Trump, by the Attorney General’s account taught by instructors he had not chosen, one of whom had met him. Trump denied the allegations throughout and cited a 98 percent internal approval figure that the plaintiffs argued was solicited under pressure. On November 18, 2016, ten days after he won the presidency and ten days before trial, the parties settled all three cases for $25 million, with no admission of wrongdoing; the court estimated claiming students would recover roughly 80 to 90 percent of what they had paid. The settlement and its approval are documented and adjudicated as such; the fraud allegations were never adjudicated, settlement having ended the cases before any verdict, and this report files them as allegations resolved by payment, no more and no less.

The Donald J. Trump Foundation, formed in 1988, closed on two records: the Washington Post’s 2016 examination of its tax filings—$20,000 in 2007 for a six-foot portrait of Trump at a charity auction, $10,000 in 2014 for a second, $12,000 in 2012 for a signed football helmet and jersey, $258,000 applied to settle legal obligations of his businesses, and a $25,000 contribution in 2013 to a political group supporting Florida’s attorney general, whose office was then weighing whether to join the Trump University investigation, for which the foundation’s own tax form answered yes to a question about prohibited self-dealing and paid a $2,500 excise tax—and the Attorney General’s suit of June 2018. The foundation stipulated in December 2018 to dissolve under court supervision. On November 7, 2019, Justice Saliann Scarpulla ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages, finding he had breached his fiduciary duty by allowing a January 2016 veterans fundraiser to be run by his campaign for political purposes; the settlement stipulations carried nineteen paragraphs of factual admissions, including that the board had not met since 1999 and that the foundation had engaged in the related-party transactions described. He paid the $2 million to eight named charities in December 2019, and the foundation’s remaining $1.8 million was distributed with it. It was a civil charity-enforcement action; no criminal charges were brought in the matter. The court characterized the $2 million as damages, not a fine, and the report follows the court.

7. The Personal Life Record

He has been married three times. Ivana Zelníčková, a Czech model, married him in 1977; their children are Donald Jr., Ivanka, and Eric. The marriage ended in a divorce decree of December 12, 1990, granted on grounds of cruel and inhuman treatment. One allegation from that proceeding requires its label stated exactly: in a divorce deposition, Ivana Trump described a 1989 incident using the word “rape”; in a statement issued in 1993 she said she had not meant the word “in a literal or criminal sense,” and she did not repeat the claim. The deposition remains sealed; its only public text is the reported excerpts and her clarification, and the matter stands in the record as withdrawn and clarified, which is how this report files it. Marla Maples, whom he married in 1993, is the mother of Tiffany; they divorced in 1999. Melania Knauss, a Slovenian model who immigrated in 1996, married him in January 2005; their son Barron was born in 2006. She is the sitting First Lady. His stated habits are documented by his own repeated statements and by the White House physicians’ reports of his terms: he does not drink alcohol and has said he never has, a position he attributes to his brother Fred Jr.’s death; he does not smoke; his physicians’ summaries of record are public documents of each term. Descriptions of his personality by associates, friendly and hostile, are attributed opinion and are excluded from this report by its method, which admits the record and not the portraiture.

8. The First Presidency: 2016, the Mueller Report, Two Impeachments, the Pandemic

He announced his candidacy on June 16, 2015, at Trump Tower. The campaign’s documented milestones include the publication on October 7, 2016, of the Access Hollywood recording of 2005, in which he described kissing and groping women without consent in terms the record quotes and this report summarizes; he apologized for the words in a video statement the same night and dismissed them as locker-room talk, both statements documented. On November 8, 2016, he was elected with 304 electoral votes after faithless electors, against 227, and lost the national popular vote by 2,868,686 votes. He was inaugurated on January 20, 2017.

The first term’s major documented acts, in brief: the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of December 2017, cutting the corporate rate permanently from 35 percent to 21 percent, with a Congressional Budget Office estimate of about $1.5 trillion added to ten-year deficits before feedback; three Supreme Court appointments—Gorsuch, confirmed 54 to 45; Kavanaugh, 50 to 48, after hearings at which Christine Blasey Ford testified alleging a sexual assault in the early 1980s, which Kavanaugh denied categorically under oath and which was not adjudicated; Barrett, 52 to 48, confirmed eight days before the 2020 election—producing a 6-to-3 majority of Republican-appointed justices, with 234 Article III judges confirmed in the term; an entry-restriction program enjoined twice and upheld in its third form by the Supreme Court, 5 to 4, in Trump v. Hawaii in June 2018; a family-separation practice under the April 2018 zero-tolerance prosecution policy, ended by his own executive order of June 20, 2018, and enjoined by a federal judge six days later, with the separated children counted at 2,342 in the administration’s spring-2018 window and at 5,300 to 5,500 across 2017 to 2020 on the Congressional Research Service’s reconciliation—the range is the period definitions, and it is printed with them; the Abraham Accords of September 2020, the first Israel–Arab normalizations since 1994; three meetings with Kim Jong Un, the first between a sitting president and a North Korean leader, producing a joint statement with no timetable, inventory, or verification mechanism and no denuclearization agreement; and the pandemic, whose United States death toll on the Johns Hopkins tally passed 400,000 on the term’s last full day, the milestones of which—the emergency declarations, the CARES Act’s $2.2 trillion, Operation Warp Speed, his hospitalization at Walter Reed in October 2020, the first vaccine authorizations that December—are documented chronology, and whose quality of response is contested along partisan lines and adjudicated nowhere, and is therefore filed as milestones only.

The Mueller investigation ran from May 17, 2017, to March 22, 2019, and produced charges against 34 individuals and three companies, eight guilty pleas, and a trial conviction. Its report’s two volumes hold the sentences by which this report quotes it. Volume I’s opening finding: “The Russian government interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion.” On coordination, verbatim: “[T]he investigation did not establish that members of the Trump Campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities.” The report stated that the campaign expected to benefit electorally from information stolen and released through Russian efforts, and that deleted communications, encrypted messaging, and false statements limited some lines of inquiry; “did not establish” is the report’s formulation, and it did not state that coordination affirmatively did not occur. Volume II, declining a traditional prosecutorial judgment on obstruction, states verbatim: “while this report does not conclude that the President committed a crime, it also does not exonerate him.” Attorney General Barr’s four-page letter of March 24, 2019, quoted the first sentence and added his own and his deputy’s conclusion that the evidence was insufficient to establish obstruction; Mueller wrote to Barr on March 27 that the letter “did not fully capture the context, nature, and substance of this Office’s work and conclusions” and that public confusion had resulted. Trump’s characterization of the report as a “complete and total exoneration” is his statement, printed against the report’s own no-exoneration sentence, which stands two paragraphs above this one.

The first impeachment arose from the July 25, 2019, call with President Zelensky of Ukraine, the administration’s hold on $391 million of appropriated security assistance—which the Government Accountability Office later ruled violated the Impoundment Control Act—and the request in the call, after Zelensky raised buying Javelin missiles, that Zelensky “do us a favor though” and look into the CrowdStrike matter and “the other thing,” the Bidens.
